title: Keeping gas supply projects in the slowest approval lane conflicts with the government's reliance on new gas for firming and for the reservation scheme
oneLiner: The industry's objection to the exclusion, and the point where the energy and environment debates meet.
body: The market operator's plan keeps gas-fired generation as firming through the 2030s, and the east-coast reservation scheme depends on new supply coming on. Excluding gas projects from streamlined assessment means the supply the government is counting on faces the longest process in the system.
contextBackground: Both halves of this claim are government policy; the tension between them is the argument.
contextDisagreement: Environment groups answer that the streamlined pathway was never meant for the highest-impact projects and that gas supply shortfalls are a reason to build storage faster, not to assess gas fields less.

otherClaim.title: Coal, gas and petroleum projects should be excluded from the streamlined approval pathway and the national-interest exemption

claimItself.title: Coal, gas and petroleum projects should be excluded from the streamlined approval pathway and the national-interest exemption
claimItself.oneLiner: The Greens' condition for passing the reforms, now law: the projects with the largest impacts keep the full assessment.
claimItself.body: Under this proposal, adopted as part of the Labor–Greens deal on 28 November 2025, coal, gas and petroleum activities, including exploration, cannot use the streamlined assessment pathway, the national-interest exemption or bioregional planning approvals. The water trigger for large coal and unconventional gas projects stays with the Commonwealth rather than being devolved to states. The case for it is that these projects carry the largest and least reversible impacts, on land, water and climate, so speed should be denied to them first. The case against is that it puts gas supply projects, which the government's own energy plan and its reservation scheme rely on, into the slowest lane in the system.

claimItself.title: AEMO's Integrated System Plan relies on gas-fired generation to firm renewables through the 2030s and beyond
claimItself.oneLiner: The market operator's own plan keeps gas peakers in the mix as backup, run for a small number of hours a year.
claimItself.body: In every Integrated System Plan scenario, gas-fired peaking plants remain in the system to cover long periods of low wind and solar output. Their capacity is held or grows while their total energy output falls, because they run rarely.
